title: Real-time updates: from one event to every open screen
dek: The two hops and when you need them, polling to WebSockets for the first, routing each update to the server holding the connection for the second, the deep dives (reconnection, huge fan-out, ordering), and the whole path at scale.

body.x: Picture two people editing the same document. When one types a letter, the other should see it within a fraction of a second. If every open editor asked the server 'anything new?' every few milliseconds, the servers would drown in requests that almost always answer 'no'.

The root of it is how HTTP works: the client sends a request, the server answers, and the exchange is over. That suits loading pages, but the server has no way to start a conversation, so it can't tell a client something changed. Real-time features need either a persistent connection that the server can write to, or a clever way of asking that wastes little.

Many engineers never build this part themselves: in most companies a specialist team built it once, and everyone else uses it. Experienced candidates are often surprised by these questions for exactly that reason. This article covers the decisions you need to make, without assuming you've built one.

items: Chat and messaging: new messages, typing indicators, read receipts.
Tracking: a rider or driver moving on the map, a delivery's status.
Live prices and auctions: stock tickers, bids, flash-sale stock counts.
Collaboration: shared documents, whiteboards, multiplayer games and chess.
Live events: comments and reactions during a stream, a ticket queue's position.
AI chat: an answer streamed to the screen word by word as it's generated.

body.x: Every real-time design has two separate parts, and it helps to say so out loud:

items: The first hop: from the server to the client. Which kind of connection carries updates to the phone or browser: polling, long polling, server-sent events, WebSockets or WebRTC.

The second hop: from the source to the server. When a rider's location changes or a message is sent, how does that update reach the particular server that holds the receiving user's open connection, among many servers?

body.cap: A message from Asha to Ravi takes two hops: from the chat service to the connection server holding Ravi's open connection, then down that connection to his phone.

body.x: The two hops have different trade-offs and are chosen separately. The parts below take them in turn: 'The first hop' covers connection types; 'The second hop' covers routing updates to the right server; the deep dives cover reconnection, huge fan-out and ordering. The last part, 'Live updates at scale', is the short version of all three.

items: If users can wait a minute, poll or just reload: a dashboard refreshed every 60 seconds is simpler than a live connection and costs almost nothing.
If updates are rare and users aren't looking at the screen, use push notifications through the phone's notification service instead of keeping a connection open.
Persistent connections cost memory, file descriptors and load-balancer capacity per user, and make deploys and scaling harder. Spend that only where the product needs it.
Ask how fresh the data must be before choosing a technique; 'within seconds' and 'within a minute' lead to different designs.
Name the two hops and decide each one separately.
Bring up failure early: connections drop, so the client must be able to reconnect and catch up.

body.x: These options are all built from the same layers (the Networking essentials concept covers them in detail):

items: Network layer (layer 3): IP moves packets from one address to another on a best-effort basis: packets can be lost, duplicated or arrive out of order.

Transport layer (layer 4): TCP sets up a connection and delivers bytes reliably and in order, at the cost of a handshake and per-connection state. UDP just sends packets with no setup and no guarantees.
Application layer (layer 7): DNS, HTTP, WebSockets and WebRTC's signalling sit on top. Nearly everything here runs over TCP; WebRTC's media runs over UDP.

body.x: Loading a page shows them working together: DNS turns the name into an IP address, TCP (and TLS) set up a connection, the HTTP request and response travel over it, and the connection is closed or kept for the next request. Every real-time option is a different way of using that connection.

body.cap: One request is four exchanges: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP. On a phone, the round trips around the server's own work are often larger than the work itself.

body.x: The client asks 'anything new?' every few seconds with an ordinary request.

items: Simple: plain HTTP, no special servers, works everywhere, every server stays stateless.
Always up to one interval late, and most requests return nothing. Ten lakh clients polling every 5 seconds is 2 lakh requests a second, mostly empty.
Good enough more often than people think: a delivery status refreshed every 10 seconds, a dashboard every minute. In an interview, it's a reasonable first answer to state and then improve.

body.x: The client sends a request, and the server holds it open until it has something to say (or a timeout of, say, 30 seconds passes), then answers. The client immediately sends the next request.

items: Updates arrive almost as soon as they happen, using only ordinary HTTP.
Each waiting client ties up a request on the server, and every message costs a full request and response, so busy streams pay a lot of overhead.
A good fit for occasional updates where you want low delay without new infrastructure, such as waiting for a payment to be confirmed.

body.cap: Polling asks on a timer and learns of an update up to one interval late. Long polling keeps a request waiting, so the answer goes out the moment the update arrives.

body.x: The client makes one HTTP request, and the server keeps the response open, writing an event to it whenever there's news. The browser's EventSource handles it and reconnects automatically, telling the server the last event id it received.

body.cap: One response carries every update. If the connection is cut, the browser reconnects by itself and sends the last id it saw, so only the missed events are sent.

items: One way only: server to client. The client still uses normal requests to send anything.
Plain HTTP, so it works through most proxies and load balancers, and with HTTP/2 many streams share one connection.
Ideal for feeds, live scores, notifications, progress bars and AI answers streamed word by word.

body.x: The client starts with an HTTP request asking to upgrade, and the connection becomes a two-way channel where either side can send messages at any time, with very little overhead per message.

body.cap: After the upgrade there are no requests: either side sends a message whenever it has one, and the connection stays open.

items: The right choice for chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing and anything where clients send frequently too.
Long-lived and stateful: each connection is tied to one server, load balancers must support long connections, and deploys must move connections gracefully.
Usually run on dedicated connection servers that do little else, so the rest of the system stays stateless.

body.x: WebRTC lets two clients send audio, video or data directly to each other, peer to peer, mostly over UDP. A signalling server helps them find each other; STUN servers help them discover their public addresses; TURN servers relay the traffic when a direct path is impossible.

body.cap: Setting up a call: signalling introduces the phones, each learns its public address, then they connect directly, with a TURN relay as the fallback.

items: For calls and video meetings, where low delay matters more than every packet arriving.
Complex to run and rarely the answer for ordinary updates; in an interview, mention it for calls or peer-to-peer features only.

items: Start from the requirement: how fresh, and does the client also send often?
Choose the simplest that fits: polling, then SSE for one-way streams, then WebSockets for two-way.
Mention the cost of open connections and that they live on their own connection servers.

body.x: Ravi's phone holds a WebSocket to one of fifty connection servers. Asha sends him a message, which arrives at the chat service. The chat service has to get the message to whichever of the fifty servers holds Ravi's connection, and it doesn't know which one that is. That routing is the second hop.
Each connection server periodically asks the database (or a queue) for new updates for the users connected to it, and pushes what it finds.

items: Simple, and the database stays the single source of truth.
Updates wait for the next poll, and fifty servers polling for lakhs of users puts constant load on the database.
Acceptable when updates are infrequent or a few seconds' delay is fine; otherwise push.

body.x: Assign each user to a connection server by hashing the user id onto a ring of servers. A client connects (or is redirected) to its assigned server, and any service with an update for Ravi computes the same hash and sends it straight there.

body.cap: Ravi's id hashes to connection server 3, so his phone connects there and the chat service sends his messages there directly. No lookup, no broadcast.

items: Routing needs no lookup table and no broadcast: everyone can compute where a user lives.
It suits servers that keep state per user or per room, such as a document's editing session or a game, so all of its clients and its state share one server.

Adding or removing a server moves some users, who must reconnect; a coordinator (ZooKeeper or etcd) keeps every service's view of the ring consistent. The Consistent hashing concept explains the ring.

body.x: A connection server subscribes, on a pub/sub broker, to a channel for each user connected to it (for example `user:ravi`). A service with an update publishes it to that channel; the broker delivers it to whichever server subscribed. When Ravi reconnects to a different server, that server subscribes instead.

body.cap: Connection servers subscribe to the channels of the users they hold. The chat service publishes to `user:ravi` without knowing where Ravi is; the broker delivers it to server 2.

items: Publishers and connection servers are decoupled: nobody needs to know where a user is connected, and servers can come and go freely.

Brokers: Redis pub/sub (fast, but drops messages for disconnected subscribers), Redis Streams or Kafka (durable, replayable), or managed services. The broker becomes critical infrastructure and must scale with the number of channels and messages.
This is the most common answer in interviews for chat, notifications and live tracking.

body.x: A close variant keeps a registry instead of channels: when a user connects, their connection server records user → server in Redis, and a service with an update looks the server up and sends it there directly. It needs one lookup per update and careful cleanup when servers die, but no broker.

body.cap: A registry turns 'customer 77' into 'server C2', so an update goes to one connection server instead of all of them.

items: Say how an update finds the right connection server; it's the part candidates most often skip.
Default to pub/sub with a channel per user or per room; mention the broker you'd use and whether it must be durable.
Use consistent hashing when the server keeps state for a room or document, and say how reconnects work when servers change.

body.x: Phones switch networks, go into tunnels and sleep; servers restart for deploys. A real-time design must assume every connection will drop and come back.

items: Detect dead connections: the client and server exchange small heartbeats (every 20 to 30 seconds) so both notice a silent drop quickly and clean up.
Reconnect politely: retry with exponential backoff and random jitter, so a server restart doesn't bring every client back in the same second.

Catch up: give every update a sequence number per user or per conversation. On reconnect, the client sends the last number it saw (SSE has a built-in Last-Event-ID header) and the server replays what came after from a durable store, not from the connection server's memory.
Make updates idempotent or deduplicate by id, because a replay can repeat something already shown.

body.cap: The phone remembers the last number it saw and the server keeps recent updates for a while, so a tunnel costs a few seconds of delay, not a missed update.

body.x: A celebrity with millions of followers posts; a final-over wicket happens with crores watching. Pushing that one update separately to every follower through one publisher and one channel would overwhelm the path. The answers:

items: Fan out in layers: publish once to a topic; each connection server subscribes once to the topic and fans out locally to its own connected viewers. A million viewers on 500 servers means 500 deliveries from the broker, then local pushes.
Pull for broadcast content: for a celebrity's post, don't push to every follower; let followers' feeds fetch it when they open the app (fan-out on read), as feed designs do for very popular accounts.

Batch and sample: for live comments or reactions, send viewers a batch every second instead of every message, and when there are thousands a second, show a sample. Nobody can read 10,000 comments a second anyway.
Cache the state: for live scores, push a small 'score changed' signal and let clients fetch the new state from a CDN or cache that absorbs the burst.

body.cap: One wicket, crores of viewers: the update is published once, each connection server receives it once, and each pushes it to its own viewers. The broker sends hundreds of messages, not crores.

body.x: Messages pass through several services and servers, any of which may delay one. Two messages sent a millisecond apart can arrive in the wrong order, which matters in a chat ('ok' before the question) or a document (edits applied out of order).

items: Order only where it matters: within one conversation, one document, one order's status. Global ordering across everything is expensive and almost never needed.
Keep one ordered path per key: route all of a conversation's messages through the same partition (Kafka keyed by conversation id) or the same server, so they stay in sequence.

Number them: the owner of the conversation assigns an increasing sequence number to each message; clients display by sequence number and hold back a message until the earlier ones have arrived or a short wait has passed.
For collaborative editing, where many people edit at once, ordering alone isn't enough: operational transforms or CRDTs merge concurrent edits so everyone converges on the same document.

body.cap: Two messages take different paths and arrive swapped. Each carries a sequence number from the conversation's owner, so the client puts them back in order before showing them.

items: For reconnection: heartbeats, backoff with jitter, sequence numbers and replay from a durable store.
For huge fan-out: publish once, fan out per server, batch or sample, and let broadcast content be pulled from a cache or CDN.
For ordering: order per conversation or document, through one partition, with sequence numbers the client sorts by.

body.x: The part 'The first hop' above compares polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets for the hop between a server and a phone. At scale the harder part is the hop before it. The update happens in the order service, but the customer's connection lives on one of hundreds of connection servers, and something has to carry the update from one to the other.

items: Connection servers do one job: hold open connections, tens of thousands each, and pass messages along. Keeping them apart from the API servers means deploying the API doesn't drop every customer's connection.
A load balancer spreads new connections over them. For WebSockets it has to support long-lived connections and keep each one on the same server for its whole life.
Each open connection costs memory for buffers and state, a few to tens of kilobytes, and a little CPU for keep-alive pings. Memory, not CPU, usually decides how many fit on one machine.
When a connection server restarts, its phones reconnect elsewhere. Restart servers one at a time, and make phones wait a random moment before reconnecting so they don't all arrive at once.

body.x: Routing an update to the right server

body.cap: One update, one phone. The registry turns 'customer 77' into 'server C2', so the event goes to one connection server instead of all of them.

body.x: A score change during a cricket final is one update for crores of phones. Routing it per user would mean crores of messages through the broker. Instead, each connection server subscribes once to the match's topic and sends the update to its own viewers: one message per server, not per viewer. When there are more connection servers than one broker can feed, add a layer of relays in between, each feeding a few hundred servers.

For values that change many times a second, such as a rider's location, send the latest value at a steady pace, every 2 to 4 seconds, instead of every change. The app moves the rider smoothly between points.

body.cap: The phone remembers the last number it saw, and the server keeps recent updates for a while. A tunnel then costs a few seconds of delay, not a missed 'your order is here'.

items: Number updates per user or per stream, and keep recent ones in a short log (a Redis stream, Kafka or a table) for as long as a phone might reasonably be away.

On reconnecting, the phone sends the last number it saw; the server replays what came after and then switches to live. Server-sent events have this built in: the browser sends a `Last-Event-ID` header when it reconnects.
If the phone was away longer than the log keeps, tell it to reload the whole state from the API instead.
Reconnect with backoff and jitter: wait 1, 2, 4 seconds and so on, plus a random part, so a server restart doesn't bring every phone back in the same second.
Treat the live channel as a way to stay fresh, not as the source of truth. The order screen still loads the order from the API when it opens.

body.x: 'Rider online' and 'typing…' use the same machinery in reverse. The connection server notes when a user connects and refreshes it every 30 seconds or so. Store presence with a short expiry, so the users of a server that crashed go offline by themselves instead of looking online forever.

A closed app has no connection. Updates that must reach the user anyway, such as 'your order is at the door', go through the phone platform's push service (APNs on iPhone, FCM on Android). Delivery there can be delayed or dropped, so the app must never rely on it: when it opens, it loads the current state from the API.

items: Choose the last hop from the direction and rate of updates: server-sent events for one-way status, WebSockets for chat or collaboration.
Draw connection servers separately, with a registry or channels that route each update to the right one.
Say what happens when a connection drops: numbered updates, a short replay log, and a full reload when the phone is too far behind.
Estimate the connections: 10 lakh customers tracking orders at dinner, at 50,000 per server, is 20 servers, plus spare ones so a failure doesn't overload the rest.

body.label: Go deeper: how many connections one machine holds

body.x: The famous limit of 65,535 ports doesn't cap connections to a server: it limits connections between one client address and one server address and port. A server's real limits are file descriptors, kernel buffers and the app's own state per connection. With small buffers and an event loop, one machine can hold hundreds of thousands of mostly idle connections.
Plan for far fewer, tens of thousands per server, so that one server's failure sends a manageable number of phones reconnecting to the others.
